query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, controlled amount of a ductile, high‐melting‐point element (e.g., Nb) to promote the in‐situ formation of finely dispersed Nb‐rich precipitates along grain boundaries in (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will improve its mechanical integrity (i.e. elevate compressive strength and crack resistance) without diminishing its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy exhibits a large caloric effect under applied magnetic and pressure fields but shows poor integrity and tends to crack.
generation.intervention: Introduce a ~5 vol% Nb addition during alloy synthesis (via controlled alloying conditions) such that Nb-rich precipitates form in situ along grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Testing under similar applied-field and pressure-field conditions as the original caloric measurements, with operational temperatures and mechanical loading regimes typical for the intended application. Processing should avoid excessive precipitate coarsening to maintain a fine microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: The Nb-rich precipitates distributed at or near the grain boundaries act as crack arresters and promote a refined microstructure. This hierarchical microstructure improves load distribution and reduces crack propagation while keeping the primary matrix intact for caloric switching.
generation.mechanism: The Nb addition facilitates a dual role: (1) mechanical reinforcement by enhancing grain-boundary cohesion and providing obstacle sites for crack propagation (thereby increasing compressive strength and toughness) and (2) maintaining the inherent rearrangements (such as order–disorder or magnetostructural transitions) that underpin the alloy’s caloric response because the Nb-rich phase is inert with respect to the caloric mechanism.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unchanged alloy (which shows compressive strengths in the range demonstrated by epoxy composites of 152–218 MPa), the Nb-modified composite is expected to exhibit an increased compressive strength (potentially reaching or exceeding ~250 MPa) and improved crack resistance while keeping the magnitude of the caloric temperature change essentially unchanged within a 10% margin.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy shows a large caloric response but poor integrity. Prior composite approaches using epoxies or low-melting In have resulted in either higher strength (up to ~218 MPa) or improved heat transport, but not both simultaneously.
generation.boundary: This intervention should work under the same applied-field, pressure-field, and temperature regimes used for caloric operation, provided the Nb content remains low enough (around 5 vol%) so that the precipitates are finely dispersed and do not percolate. Excessive addition may lead to overly stiffening the alloy or altering the caloric mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The precise Nb level required to optimize integrity without affecting the caloric performance, and whether Nb is the best element choice compared to other ductile options, requires experimental verification. There is also some uncertainty whether the in-situ precipitates might slightly alter the local transformation dynamics.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples: one set with ~5 vol% Nb added under controlled processing to form fine Nb-rich precipitates, and a control set without Nb. Subject both sets to identical applied magnetic and pressure fields, along with standard compressive and fracture testing. Use microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM, XRD) to verify the formation and distribution of the Nb-rich phase.
measurements: Caloric response magnitude (temperature change under applied field/pressure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-modified alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength or fracture toughness) relative to the control, or if its caloric response is reduced by more than approximately 10% compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.
